Magma. Molten rock beneath Earth's crust—the parent material for all igneous rocks and volcanic lava. When magma remains underground, it cools slowly to form coarse-grained plutonic rocks. When it erupts through volcanoes, it cools rapidly as lava, creating fine-grained volcanic rocks. Understanding magma composition, temperature, and viscosity is essential to predicting volcanic behavior and interpreting Earth's internal chemistry.

Magma forms primarily at divergent plate boundaries, such as mid-ocean ridges, and at convergent boundaries such as subduction zones, where pressure and temperature lower the melting point of rock. Composition varies widely. Basaltic magma has low silica, erupts at approximately 1200 degrees Celsius, flows freely, and erupts as shield volcanoes. Rhyolitic magma has high silica, erupts at approximately 900 degrees Celsius, and is thick and explosive.

Magma is lighter than the solid rock surrounding it, creating buoyancy that drives it upward through cracks and weak zones in the crust. Crystallization begins as magma cools. Minerals with high melting points crystallize first—olivine and pyroxene—followed by lower-melting minerals like feldspar and quartz. Fractional crystallization and magma mixing can change composition, explaining how different eruption products emerge from the same magma chamber.

The presence of dissolved water and other volatiles dramatically lowers magma viscosity and can trigger explosive degassing during eruption. Ancient magma, now cooled to solid rock, preserves information about early Earth. Its composition reveals the mantle's chemical evolution. Magma chambers act as thermal reservoirs, accumulating beneath volcanoes and building pressure that eventually triggers eruption when overpressure exceeds rock strength.

The viscosity of magma determines eruptive style. Low-viscosity basaltic magma produces gentle effusive eruptions, while high-viscosity rhyolitic magma creates violent explosive events. Partial melting of the mantle beneath mid-ocean ridges produces new oceanic crust that continuously spreads, a process driven by convection of magma and rock. Erupted lava flows cool into basalt. Slower cooling of magma underground produces plutonic rocks like granite, preserving a record of the magma's composition.

The volcano is the surface expression where magma erupts as lava and pyroclastic material. Igneous rock forms when magma cools, either underground as plutonic rock or above ground as volcanic rock. Plate tectonics is the mechanism that generates most magma through decompression melting and subduction. Minerals are the crystalline phases that form as magma cools in a predictable sequence. Lava is the extrusive form of magma that erupts onto Earth's surface. Basalt is the most common volcanic rock, formed from rapid cooling of basaltic magma.
